title: AI Set to Extend Fossil Fuel Dominance, Research Warns — And Not Because of Data Centers
excerpt: A new paper finds AI's biggest climate impact comes from making oil-and-gas production cheaper, while surging data center demand drives a fossil fuel infrastructure boom.
body:
• A new research paper finds AI's biggest climate impact will come from making fossil fuel production cheaper and more efficient, not from data center power consumption
  • AI-enabled productivity gains could increase global CO2 emissions by 0.47 to 1.8 billion tons annually — equivalent to Mexico's entire annual output at the lower end
  • The IEA reports US investment in fossil-fuel power plants will overtake China's in 2026, driven by a threefold increase in gas-power spending linked to data centers
  • Global orders for new gas-power plants hit 130 gigawatts in 2025, a 25-year high, with US demand a major factor

The conventional debate about artificial intelligence and climate change has focused on data centers — their enormous electricity consumption, their strain on power grids, their push for new energy sources. But a growing body of research suggests that framing misses the bigger picture entirely.

A paper published in the journal npj Climate Action argues that AI's most profound energy impact will not come from how the technology is powered, but from what it is used for. The core finding: by making oil-and-gas production cheaper and more efficient, AI is on course to extend the dominance of fossil fuels and push global carbon dioxide emissions significantly higher.

The Oil Patch, Not the Data Center

The paper, co-authored by Holly and Will Alpine — both former Microsoft sustainability staffers who left the company over its oil-and-gas work — models what happens when AI boosts productivity across both renewable energy and fossil fuels. The result is stark: improved economics of oil-and-gas production would increase global CO2 emissions by between 0.47 billion and 1.8 billion tons per year.

https://x.com/AndyMasley/status/2088820360082764145

"On the smaller side it's about the emissions of Mexico annually."

— Holly Alpine, co-author and climate advocate

The mechanism is already visible in corporate earnings reports. Oil-and-gas companies routinely highlight how AI scans geological data and optimizes production. ExxonMobil recently disclosed that an AI model identified four drilling prospects in Guyana that conventional methods had missed entirely. Consulting firm Wood Mackenzie estimates AI could unlock another trillion barrels of oil, while Goldman Sachs predicts widespread adoption could slash capital expenditure and reduce oil prices by up to 1 per barrel.

A Surge in Fossil Fuel Infrastructure

Simultaneously, the sheer electricity demands of AI data centers are driving a parallel boom in fossil fuel infrastructure. According to the International Energy Agency, US investment in fossil-fuelled power plants is set to overtake China's in 2026 — a reversal driven almost entirely by the data center buildout.

US gas-power investment tripled in 2025, and the IEA expects this trend to continue through 2026. Globally, orders for new gas-power plants reached 130 gigawatts in 2025, a 25-year high, with US demand cited as a "major factor." More than 85 gas-powered facilities are currently under construction worldwide to meet AI's energy appetite, according to Global Energy Monitor.

The numbers keep escalating. Amazon recently announced a data center project in Texas with permission to tap 7.65 gigawatts of gas power. Google has acknowledged its carbon emissions have risen 48 percent over five years, largely due to AI integration. Climate scientist Zeke Hausfather has estimated that AI agents could consume 600 times more energy than standard prompts.

The Counterargument

Not everyone agrees AI will inevitably entrench fossil fuels. Artem Abramov, deputy head of analysis at Rystad Energy, argues the Alpines may underestimate how AI could accelerate improvements in low-carbon technologies. He acknowledges AI will bring savings for oil-and-gas producers but questions whether those savings will translate into more production or simply better investor returns.

"Those savings flow mainly to investor returns, not incremental barrels," Abramov said.

BloombergNEF projects solar will become the world's largest power source by 2035, and the tech sector accounts for roughly 40 percent of all corporate power-purchase agreements — many of which support emerging clean technologies like small modular nuclear reactors and advanced geothermal.

What It Means for Tech Workers and the Diaspora

The findings carry particular weight for Indian-American professionals in the tech industry, many of whom work at the very companies driving both AI expansion and corporate sustainability pledges. The tension between building AI products and their downstream climate effects is increasingly difficult to reconcile — a friction the Alpines experienced firsthand at Microsoft before leaving to advocate for limits on AI's use in growing fossil fuel production.

As US electricity demand is projected to rise 2 percent annually through 2030, with data centers accounting for half that increase, the industry faces a fundamental question: whether AI's productivity gains will accelerate the clean energy transition or delay it.
